# Section 3.1: Confidence Intervals

## Introduction

![](media/image1.png)Up until now, we have been using hypothesis tests to determine if a value for a parameter is plausible. Our new goal is **estimation**: what values of the parameter are plausible?

![](media/image2.png)![](media/image3.png)**Confidence Interval:** a range of likely values for the \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

![](media/image4.png)

## Example: Legalization of Medical Marijuana

In February of 2014, a Star Tribune Minnesota poll asked a random sample of adults in Minnesota, "Do you support or oppose legalizing marijuana for medical purposes in Minnesota?" Of the 800 adults surveyed, 408 (51%) answered that they would support this.

Ultimately, the Star Tribune conducted this poll because they wanted to estimate the proportion of adults in Minnesota that felt (at the time of the survey) that medical marijuana should be legalized. Keep this in mind as you answer the following questions.

## General Form of a Confidence Interval

Notice how the confidence interval is centered around the point estimate.

![](media/image79.png)![](media/image80.png)

$$\text{Confidence Interval (CI)}\mathbf{=}\text{Point Estimate}\mathbf{\pm}\text{Margin of Error}$$

In the previous example, the confidence interval can be expressed as:

![](media/image81.png)51% ± 3.5% (i.e., 47.5% ≤ π ≤ 54.5%).

![](media/image82.png)![](media/image83.png)

## Significance Levels ($\alpha$)

![](media/image84.png)Significance Level + Confidence Level = 100%

When $\alpha = 0.10$,

- Relates to a 90% CI

- Rejects when p-value \< 0.10

- Narrower than 95% CI

- Rejects the null more often (remember than $\alpha = 0.10$ means that we reject the null 10 percent of the time)

![](media/image85.png)![](media/image86.png)

![](media/image87.png)![](media/image88.png)![](media/image89.png)![](media/image90.png)

When $\alpha = 0.05$,

- Relates to a 95% CI

- Rejects when p-value \< 0.05

When $\alpha = 0.01$,

- Relates to a 99% CI

- Rejects when p-value \< 0.01

- Wider than 95% CI

- Rejects the null less often than 95% CI

## Technical Note About Confidence Intervals

![](media/image95.png)![](media/image96.png)We say that we are "$100 - \alpha*100\%$ confident" because $100 - \alpha*100\%$ of the confidence intervals generated from samples of a given population will cover the true parameter value. In the instance of $\alpha = 0.05$, this means that 95% of confidence intervals generated from samples within a population will cover the true parameter value. In Section 3.3, we will look at an applet that will demonstrate what this means. This is NOT the same as saying that the probability of the parameter being in the confidence interval is $100 - \alpha*100\%$

![](media/image97.png)![](media/image98.png)![](media/image99.png)![](media/image100.png)![](media/image101.png)![](media/image102.png)![](media/image103.png)![](media/image104.png)![](media/image105.png)![](media/image106.png)![](media/image107.png)![](media/image108.png)

# ![](media/image109.png)Section 3.2: Confidence Intervals for One Proportion

## ![](media/image110.png)Formula

The general formula for confidence intervals is as follows:

$$\text{Observed Statistic} \pm \text{Multiplier} \cdot \text{Standard Error}$$

![](media/image111.png)

Unlike in Chapter 1, we now have a new formula for the standard error:

![](media/image112.png)![](media/image113.png)

$$SE = \sqrt{\frac{\widehat{p} \cdot \left( 1 - \widehat{p} \right)}{n}}$$

Notice how we are no longer using π in the calculation, but rather $\widehat{p}$.

To construct a 95% Confidence interval, the multiplier we will use in this course is 2. This gives us the confidence interval for one proportions to be:

![](media/image114.png)

$$\mathbf{CI =}\widehat{\mathbf{p\ }}\mathbf{\pm 2*\ }\sqrt{\frac{\widehat{\mathbf{p}}\mathbf{*}\left( \mathbf{1 -}\widehat{\mathbf{p}} \right)}{\mathbf{n}}}\mathbf{= (Lower\ Limit,\ Upper\ Limit)}$$

![](media/image115.png)Technical aside: if you look into confidence intervals from sources outside of our class, you will notice that the multiplier value for a 95% confidence interval will likely be 1.96. However, we will [only use a multiplier value of 2 for this course.]{.underline}

## Conclusions Based Off of Confidence Intervals

Recall the general interpretation of a confidence interval.

- We are 95% confident that the long run proportion of *"context"* falls between (*lower limit*) and (*upper limit*).

![](media/image134.png)If the null hypothesis value is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ of the interval

- It is a likely value

- Fail to Reject

![](media/image135.png)If the null hypothesis value is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ of the interval

- It is not a likely value

- Reject

Conclusion: We (do/do not) have evidence to conclude (restate alternative in context).

In the context of the medical marijuana example,

- ![](media/image136.png)![](media/image137.png)![](media/image138.png)![](media/image139.png)Hypothesis

  - $H_{O}:\pi = 0.5$

  - $H_{A}:\pi \neq 0.5$

- Confidence Interval

  - $(0.47,\ 0.55) \rightarrow Fail\ to\ Reject\ since\ 0.5\ falls\ inside\ our\ interval$

> ![](media/image140.png)

  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ![](media/image141.png)           ![](media/image142.png)           ![](media/image143.png)
  ------------------------- ------- ------------------------- ------- -------------------------

  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

> ![](media/image144.png)![](media/image145.png)

- Interpretation of Confidence Interval

  - We are 95% confident the long run proportion of adults in Minnesota who feel medical marijuana should be legalized falls between 0.47 and 0.55.

- Conclusion in context

  - We do not have evidence to conclude the long run proportion of adults in Minnesota who feel medical marijuana should be legalized is different from 0.5

## ![](media/image146.png)Conclusions

  ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                          **P-value**     **Standardized Statistic**         **Confidence Interval**
  -------------------- ----------------- ---------------------------- --------------------------------------
       **Reject**           \< 0.05           "Outside the 2's"        Hypothesized value outside of the CI

   **Fail to Reject**       \> 0.05           "Between the 2's"        Hypothesized value inside of the CI
  ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# ![](media/image147.png)Section 3.3: Confidence Intervals for Single Means

## Formula

The general formula for confidence intervals also applies to single means.

![](media/image148.png)

$$Observed\ Statistic\  \pm \ Multiplier\ *\ Standard\ Error$$

Before calculating the confidence interval, be sure that the validity conditions are met for the theory approach (sample size greater than 20 and the distribution is not strongly skewed).

The formula for the standard error is the same as from Chapter 2.

![](media/image149.png)

$$SE = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$$

95% Confidence interval

$$\mathbf{CI =}\overline{\mathbf{x}}\mathbf{\pm 2*}\frac{\mathbf{s}}{\sqrt{\mathbf{n}}}\mathbf{= (Lower\ Limit,\ Upper\ Limit)}$$

![](media/image150.png)

This applet simulates drawing random samples from a known population (a luxury that we almost never have in practice). The "Study Replications" is the number of samples that you draw from the population and calculate the confidence interval.

![Chart Description automatically generated](media/image191.png){width="4.383561898512686in" height="2.6914884076990377in"}

In this instance, the confidence interval calculated from the sample covered the true population mean of 150. Suppose now that we change the "Study Replications" to 5.

![Chart, box and whisker chart Description automatically generated](media/image192.png){width="4.07865157480315in" height="2.5879396325459316in"}

All 5 studies covered the population mean. With study #5, you can see that the confidence interval almost narrowly misses population mean, but it is still contained within the interval. # Section 3.4: Width of Confidence Intervals

## Factors Influencing the Confidence Interval

![](media/image193.png)![](media/image194.png)There are three factors that affect the width of a confidence interval: confidence level, sample size, and standard error.

![](media/image195.png)![](media/image196.png)![](media/image197.png)

## ![](media/image198.png)![](media/image199.png)![](media/image200.png)Confidence level

![](media/image201.png)Significance Level + Confidence Level = \_\_\_\_\_\_\_

- ![](media/image202.png)Confidence Level Increases $\rightarrow$ Significance Level \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

  - Rejecting Less Often $\rightarrow$ More Likely Values

  - Interval Widens

- ![](media/image203.png)Confidence Level Decreases $\rightarrow$ Significance Level \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

  - Rejecting More Often $\rightarrow$ Fewer Likely Values

  - Interval Narrows

  - ![](media/image204.png)"If you want to be more confident you have to cover more values."

<!-- -->

## Technical Aside

Mathematically, why do the effects of sample size and standard error make sense? Recall the standard error formulas for both proportion and means below.

![](media/image238.png)![](media/image239.png)![](media/image240.png)![](media/image241.png)![](media/image242.png)![](media/image243.png)

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
           **One Proportion**            $$SE = \sqrt{\frac{\widehat{p}\left( 1 - \widehat{p} \right)}{n}}$$
  ------------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------
   ![](media/image244.png)**One Mean**                       $$SE = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$$

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

From the general formula for the confidence interval, we know that the sample size and standard error do not affect the observed statistic or the multiplier. As the sample size increases, the denominator of the standard error increases, which decreases the value for the standard error.
